articles.title: Ford’s first ultra-cheap EV is called Fathom, a full-featured truck for $28,350
articles.summary: Fathom translates as “six feet deep,” which is probably where Ford would like to bury the Slate Truck.
articles.body: For nearly a year now, Ford has been teasing big things at low prices from its next generation of EVs, a “Model T moment” built atop a new platform assembled in an innovative way. Today, we know the name and price of the first product to take advantage of that supposed moment: a midsize electric truck called Fathom that starts at just $28,350. That’s not exactly great news for fans of the Slate Truck, the new electric upstart that’s leaning hard into its feature-free nature by painting itself as the ultimate DIY machine. Paint, though, is among the long line of modern niceties omitted to help the Slate Truck reach its starting price of $24,950. That first Slate also famously lacks things like power windows, a touchscreen, or even a basic stereo system. Ford’s Fathom, on the other hand, will be a fully featured vehicle, including integrated Apple Maps running on what’s called a “large, high-resolution touch screen.“ And, yes, both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay will be supported. [Media: Where the Slate seats two by default (an optional, $5,000 SUV kit expands that to five), the base Fathom aims to have greater interior volume than a Toyota RAV4. It’ll have an open bed out back and a frunk, too. The base Fathom will also include all the sensors needed to power Ford’s hands-free Blue Cruise system, though actually using that service will almost definitely come at extra cost. For reference, Blue Cruise currently costs an additional $2,495 as a one-time purchase, or $495 annually. How will Ford bring all these relative luxuries to a truck that costs just $3,400 more than the Slate? They’re taking the same approach as your friendly local furniture liquidator: volume, volume, volume. Cars, trucks, and SUVs built on Ford’s Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform will come together in a new way, with the vehicle effectively split into multiple, parallel assembly lines. The front, rear, and middle of the vehicle can all be assembled in parallel, then effectively stuck together at the end before being shipped off to your local dealer with a blue oval out front. Additionally, the construction of the vehicles themselves will be simplified, reducing both component and labor costs. High-volume manufacturing plus streamlined assembly will be key to Ford making the Fathom’s suggested retail price viable. However, it was never production capacity that slowed down Ford’s EV aspirations in the past. Lack of interest from buyers and dealers have stymied the company’s prior battery-powered efforts, resulting in billions in losses and the cancellation of the F-150 Lightning. Will a new focus and lower price mean more success? The Fathom’s starting cost is close to half that of the Lightning, a factor that surely has to help. Ford says the Fathom will enter production at the company’s updated Louisville Assembly Plant next year, with deliveries happening before the end of 2027. Pre-orders open early next year. The Slate Truck, meanwhile, hits the streets later this year, giving it a roughly 12-month head start in what hopefully won’t be a four-wheeled race to the bottom.

articles.title: Should you switch back to wired headphones? Here's why Kylie Jenner and other celebrities are doing so
articles.summary: Why are so many celebrities using wired headphones? It's not because your AirPods aren't secure.
articles.body:
If you're old like me (or an aging millennial, anyway), you may have noticed a weird tech trend lately – wired headphones are making a comeback. Everyone from Kylie Jenner and Hailey Bieber to Ariana Grande and Dua Lipa have been spotted carrying or using a pair. Last week, a viral X post pointing this out spawned a wave of users across X and Reddit to speculate that celebrities know something that we, the mere masses, don't: your wireless earbuds can be hacked.

But is there any truth to that claim? Fortunately, you probably don't need to toss your $250 AirPods in the trash. Here's what you need to know.

Hate being caught with a tinfoil hat on but there's a reason why celebs wear wired headphones and not AirPods/bluetooth. — Barbra Wyre Updates✨ (@BarbraWyre) October 7, 2026

Hate being caught with a tinfoil hat on but there's a reason why celebs wear wired headphones and not AirPods/bluetooth.

Barbra Wyre Updates✨ (@BarbraWyre) October 7, 2026

Can your wireless Bluetooth earbuds be hacked?

Technically, just about anything can be hacked if someone has enough time, patience and expensive equipment to do it. The chances of a random person putting in the effort to eavesdrop on the podcast you're listening to on your morning commute are pretty slim, though.

Bluetooth – the wireless protocol that your phone uses to connect to wireless earbuds – has its vulnerabilities like anything else, but it uses various security techniques , like encryption, to make it harder for hackers to exploit. You can avoid most problems by making sure you unpair your phone from old devices you don't use anymore and always keeping your phone updated. If you want to be extra safe, you can turn off Bluetooth on your phone or laptop when you aren't using it.

The truth is, most of us aren't targets for someone who might want to use Bluetooth as a hacking vector. You're much more likely to become the victim of a phishing scheme or ransomware attack.

Instead, politicians, business executives and others who might be targets for espionage are more likely to be the targets of a Bluetooth hack. Famously, former Vice President Kamala Harris told Stephen Colbert that she uses wired "earpods" because of information she was privy to in classified briefings during her time in the Senate. "Don't be on the train using your earpods and thinking somebody can't listen to your conversation," Harris said.

So what's with the wired headphones everywhere?

In the case of celebrities wearing wired earbuds, it's indeed a trend. Y2K nostalgia is very much in right now , and what's more Y2K than wired headphones? Harper's Bazaar has declared them the "coolest it-girl accessory." And they pair up nicely with retro tech like iPods, which are making a comeback , just like cassette tapes and vinyl records before them.

There's some practicality involved too. Wired headphones don't require charging, so you'll never have a battery die mid-song. And as ABC News contributor Mike Muse said in a September segment , the wires signal that the wearer is more "cool" and "grounded" in an increasingly digital world. Given the pace of change and anxiety over AI , it's not that surprising that some folks are opting for a more analogue look with their personal tech.

So don't feel like you need to ditch your wireless earbuds out of fear of some latent security issue. But if you want to stick with what's trendy, wired earbuds are definitely having a moment.

images.caption: Why are so many celebrities using wired headphones? It's not because your AirPods aren't secure. (Moritz Scholz via Getty Images)

articles.title: Apple’s new Find My-compatible remote will also work with your old Apple TV
articles.summary: If you own any Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD, you can upgrade to the new Siri Remote with Find My for $59.
articles.body: You don’t need to buy the new Apple TV 4K just to get the updated Siri Remote with Find My and a built-in speaker, as it works with every model released going back to the Apple TV HD and is available to buy standalone for $59. Previous Siri Remotes had a basic iOS feature to help you find your misplaced remote, but this is better, with one notable catch. Now the remote has Find My support, but if you want to see exactly how far away it is on your iPhone with details like “20 feet,” rather than simply “far” or “near,” you will need to have an iPhone Duo, iPhone Air, or any iPhone 17 or later. Those are the only models that include its new N1 networking chip with support for Bluetooth channel sounding, which enables AirTag-like precision tracking, but without requiring a UWB chip. > Find My support is available on the Siri Remote (2nd generation and later). Precision Finding works on the Siri Remote (4th generation) paired with iPhone Duo, iPhone Air or iPhone 17 or later (excluding iPhone 17e) running the latest iOS software; availability varies by region. As Stephen Robles points out in a post on Threads, the new remote’s backward compatibility means only a couple of features are limited to the new Apple TV 4K, including its built-in mic and surround sound with paired HomePod speakers. It will start shipping on November 13th, the same date as the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.

articles.title: $15 gets you Psychonauts 2, the latest Like a Dragon game, and more
articles.summary: We’re highlighting deals on Humble Choice’s membership this month, as well as Borderlands 4, Valve’s Index, and preorders for Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.
articles.body: There are several deals happening right now on video games and gaming-related tech that are worth sharing. To start, this month’s Humble Choice drop of Steam PC games is really good. The $14.99 per month service is offering subscribers Like A Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii, Price of Persia: The Lost Crown, Psychonauts 2, Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor, and more. You get to keep the games forever, even if you pay just for this month. I’ve tossed around getting each of these games on Steam in the past, and it’s great to get them all here for such a low price. I’m not going to convince you to hang onto the membership any longer than you plan to, though while you have it, make sure to use it to save on digital games you were considering buying. Nintendo Switch 2 games, for example, are discounted, making Humble the place to get the cheapest prices. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is $53.99 for members, and most other full-price games are about $6 off the retail price. Other great Verge-approved deals * Valve told The Verge in late 2025 that it was no longer manufacturing the Valve Index wired virtual reality headset. The company is now running through the last of its stock and is marking down what’s left by 20 percent. The headset itself is $399.20, down from $499, replacement left controllers are $119.20 (was $149), and replacement tether cables are $103.20, down from $129. The headset requires a base station (also known as a lighthouse) in order to track, and those are unfortunately no longer available via Valve. You’ll have to hit up eBay or Craigslist to get one. Read our review of the 2019 headset. * First-person looter shooter Borderlands 4 is all the way down to $19.91 for disc editions of the Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5 title at Amazon. The price for the 2025 game is usually sitting at around $30, though this is the most affordable price to date. The latest game in the series is good at what Borderlands has always been good for: co-op multiplayer goodness. It’s still really fun to jump in with a friend to blaze through its campaign, even if the gameplay is fairly shallow. Read our review. * Lastly, whether you already saw Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey in theaters or you’ve been waiting for watch it at home, the 4K Blu-ray version is available to preorder with a small discount. Originally priced at $34.99, the set that includes a 4K Blu-ray, a standard 1080p Blu-ray, plus a digital code for the film is $29.99 at Best Buy and $29.65 at Barnes and Noble (members can save 10 percent more). If it’s your first-ever purchase on Gruv, you can get the set for $25.46 when you use the code FIRSTGRUV15 at checkout. The film launches November 17th. Read our review of seeing it in IMAX.

articles.title: HomeView doesn’t natively support any video apps yet — not even Apple’s
articles.summary: Apple TV, Apple Books audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, and Apple News Plus aren’t natively supported on the HomeView, instead requiring an iPhone connection.
articles.body: Apple says HomeView is “the perfect way” to enjoy its audio and video entertainment apps, but some notable examples like Apple TV only work if you AirPlay it through your iPhone. As noted on the HomeView spec page, Apple TV, Apple Books audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, and Apple News Plus aren’t natively supported on the smart hub, so you’ll have to use your phone to operate them. HomeView is foremostly designed as a hub for managing smart home gadgets, but competing smart display hardware like Amazon’s Echo Show and Google’s Nest Hub devices can natively stream Prime Video and YouTube, respectively, without requiring a phone connection. Apple TV is also featured in at least one promotional image for HomeView, but the AirPlay requirement is in small print on its announcement page: > “Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby.” > [Image: These are the app limitations flagged on Apple’s HomeView spec page. We have reached out to Apple for more information on why HomeView doesn’t natively support Apple TV, Apple Books audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, and Apple News Plus, and if that may change in the future. [Media: The hardware itself certainly isn’t a limitation — HomeView runs on Apple’s A18 chip, the same processor that powers an iPhone 16. Its software functions more like CarPlay than iOS, iPadOS, or even Apple TV, since, like CarPlay, it requires a connected iPhone for many functions. The HomeView also doesn’t have an App Store (which is typical for smart home hubs), which makes that CarPlay connection even more significant for third-party app developers, since apps that support projecting video or audio through the platform will work easily from day one.

articles.title: Android is using AI to suss out scammers in Google Messages
articles.summary: Android is introducing new scam defense features that aim to make it easier for users to evade mobile fraud, including bolstered protection in Google Messages.
articles.body: Android is introducing new scam defense features that aim to make it easier for users to evade mobile fraud, including bolstered protection in Google Messages and additional safeguarding tools. Building on the Scam Detection feature in Google Messages, a new “enhanced protection” setting will be rolling out in the coming weeks that taps into cloud-based Gemini AI models to quickly evaluate a potential scammer’s intentions in conversations with an unrecognized sender. “Scammers often disguise their true motives behind slow-burn conversations,” Google said in its update announcement. “This secure cloud analysis augments and extends our existing on-device detection, allowing us to identify novel and sophisticated attacks, actively uncovering and stopping abusers who try to hide their tracks.” User data is encrypted during this AI analysis and “processed in a secure dedicated space” that Google (and anyone else besides the user) can’t access. The enhanced protection mode will be opt-in, and also uses on-device Gemini Nano AI to inspect real-time web signals in unfamiliar URLs sent to the user before they’re opened to determine if the links are malicious. Additional security features announced today include blocking apps from enabling call forwarding, and notifying the user when someone attempts to do so, along with automatically concealing sensitive information while screen-sharing in Chrome and Android WebView. The scam detection feature for chat notifications Google introduced on Pixel phones last year is also expanding to devices from Honor, Motorola, Oppo, OnePlus, Realme, Tecno, Vivo, Xiaomi, and more. Google says it plans to bring it to “hundreds of millions of additional users later this year.”

articles.title: Repairing the iPhone Duo’s folding screen costs as much as a new iPhone
articles.summary: If you don’t get AppleCare Plus for the iPhone Duo, any repairs are going to be pretty expensive. Apple published the estimated repair costs for the iPhone Duo without AppleCare Plus today, including $999 for inner display damage.
articles.body: If you don’t get AppleCare Plus for the iPhone Duo, any repairs are going to be pretty expensive. Apple published the estimated repair costs for the iPhone Duo without AppleCare Plus today, as reported by MacRumors, and they can be high: Battery service, for example, will cost $229, inner display damage will cost $999, and “other damage” costs $1,499. Here’s Apple’s estimated costs for various repairs if you don’t have AppleCare Plus: > Cover layer damage $49 > Back glass damage $199 > Battery service $229 > Rear camera damage $229 > Outer display damage $379 > Outer display and back glass damage $509 > Inner display damage $999 > Other damage $1,499 With AppleCare Plus, prices are lower, including $0 for battery service, $99 to repair the inner display, and $99 for “other accidental damage.” But AppleCare Plus with Theft and Loss for the iPhone Duo is its own cost, at $19.99 per month, $199.99 per year, or a flat $399. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 and will be available on October 23rd, with preorders kicking off on Friday at 8AM ET.

articles.title: Apple’s new HomeView smart display is $10 cheaper at Amazon
articles.summary: Apple’s gray and creamy white HomeView smart displays are already on sale for $289.99 ($10 off) at Amazon ahead of their November 13th launch.
articles.body: Apple only just announced on Tuesday that its first smart display, the HomeView, will arrive on November 13th, but you can already save a couple bucks on it. Right now, you can buy the display for $289.99 ($10 off) in gray and the creamy white “starlight” colorway at Amazon. Sure, it’s a small discount, but deals on new Apple devices ahead of launch are rare. [Product: Apple HomeView | Expect a full review of the HomeView in November, but my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy spent some brief time with it and likened it to an “iPhone for your home” that looks a bit like an oversized Apple Watch. It features a gorgeous seven-inch square touchscreen that can recognize up to six household members and automatically switch between personalized experiences, displaying information relevant to whoever is using it. As you might already know, the HomeView also doubles as a smart home hub, with support for Matter and Thread. You can use it to control compatible smart home devices, view live feeds and recorded footage from HomeKit Secure Video cameras, and more. It also features a 12-megapixel FaceTime camera for video calls, and doubles as an entertainment device, letting you play music, display photos, and more. Apple’s AI-powered Siri assistant is another big part of the experience, allowing you to ask questions and get information using personal context from your messages, calendar, and emails. That means you can ask it to find your lost keys, play a song someone texted you, pull up a recipe with step-by-step instructions and built-in timers, or help you keep track of your schedule without having to reach for your phone. Read our hands-on impressions.

However, until October 19th, you can save up to twenty percent on gift cards when you buy them through the Google Play store. There are a variety of discounts and retailers available, including 20 percent off $50 at Barnes and Noble, 20 percent off $100 at REI, and 10 percent off $100 at GameStop. You don’t need an Android phone or tablet to save, but you’ll need to sign up for a Google Play account if you don’t have one already. articles.title: As a TV enthusiast, I was hoping for more from the Apple TV 4K
articles.summary: The new Apple TV 4K streaming box has a very premium price tag and doesn’t add desired home theater features.
articles.body: It’s been four long years since the last Apple TV 4K was released, and in that time there have been lots of hopes and dreams for features in whatever comes next. A new chip, 4K/120Hz support, audio passthrough, a remote locator, better home control integration — the 2022 Apple TV 4K is a great box, but there’s still plenty of room for improvement. With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K announced on Tuesday, some of those hopes were met, while others were unfortunately left out. Coloring the announcement is the device’s price. Apple eliminated the cheaper 64GB, Wi-Fi-only model, leaving just the 128GB, Wi-Fi and Ethernet model — and bumped up its price to $300. I repeat, $300 for a streaming device. It’s a hefty price when every other major streamer on the market is at least half the cost. There are new features I like about this year’s Apple TV 4K. More processing power is great — although my third generation is still running plenty fast — as is the Find My support for when the remote inevitably gets lost in the couch cushions or tangled up in blankets. Built-in far-field mics for talking to Siri are nice, too, provided you don’t stuff the box into a credenza like I do. The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K also adds a dedicated AV1 decoder, which allows for higher-quality streaming from apps that support it, such as Netflix, which is excellent. Any potential improvement to streaming content is a welcome one. My primary concern, though, is how the Apple TV 4K performs as an integral piece of my home theater. Apple added the ability to create a surround sound system by using its HomePod 2 and HomePod Mini 2 smart speakers in matching pairs for fronts and surrounds. For Apple ecosystem fans looking to build out a surround setup akin to Sonos or Bose, it’s an interesting idea (and I’m all for getting people into immersive sound in their home theaters). But as I expect is the same for many people interested in pricey streaming hardware, I already have a sound system — it’s an Atmos setup with a combination of SVS and Revel speakers. I’m not setting up my two HomePod 2s in my living room and spending another $300 on a pair of HomePod Mini 2s to replace my existing speakers. [Image: The Apple TV 4K pairs with up to four HomePods (such as the Mini 2 pictured here) for surround sound. What I, and many current users, have been hoping for from the Apple TV 4K for years is the addition of audio passthrough. This would allow my more expensive and capable audio/video receiver to decode the raw audio stream instead of the Apple TV using its Continuous Audio Connection, which can cause some playback issues. Additionally, it would have been nice to see Apple support 120fps output, especially for those who use Moonlight to stream games to it. That’s a feature that would have set the Apple TV 4K apart from all the other streamers, which top out at 60fps, and helped to justify the high price. Apple could have also used it to pivot more into TV gaming. (For movies, though, the 60fps limit is not a huge deal, as the box can be set to output 24fps, allowing a native 120Hz TV to just use 5:5 pulldown.) Other premium features that would set Apple’s streaming box apart and make home theater enthusiasts throw their money at it include an HDMI input for HDMI passthrough or a digital optical out. I understand leaving them out if it meant raising the price further. This box is already expensive enough. But it does leave the Apple TV 4K in an uncomfortable spot, pairing a high-end price with features that are largely matched elsewhere for much less. Are these high-end omissions a concern for the majority of people? Not really. But those people are going to look at the $300 price tag of the Apple TV 4K and then at Google, Roku, or Amazon streaming devices, which are all half that price or less. The Apple TV 4K is looked at as the premium streamer option, but the now extra premium price without some of the, admittedly niche, features gives me pause. Maybe the new Apple TV 4K will surprise me. I’ve certainly been looking forward to it for a while. I already appreciate the way Apple handles privacy, and if Apple adds features in coming months, maybe it could be worth it. But that $300 price? It might be better spent elsewhere in your home theater setup.
